theory.overview: Exception handling mechanisms allow programs to gracefully handle errors and exceptional conditions. The implementation involves stack unwinding, exception tables, and zero-cost exceptions (where the happy path has no overhead). Understanding these mechanisms helps write exception-safe code and debug stack traces.

keyConcepts.title: Stack Unwinding
keyConcepts.content: When an exception is thrown, the runtime searches up the call stack for a matching catch handler. Each stack frame is 'unwound' - destructors run, stack is popped - until a handler is found or the program terminates.

keyConcepts.title: Exception Tables
keyConcepts.content: Compilers generate DWARF or similar metadata mapping code addresses to exception handlers. This enables the runtime to find appropriate catch blocks during unwinding without runtime checks in the happy path.

keyConcepts.title: Zero-Cost Exceptions
keyConcepts.content: Modern C++ implementations make exceptions cost-free when not thrown. The overhead is moved to the exceptional path via lookup tables, unlike setjmp/longjmp which always pay a cost.

keyConcepts.title: Exception Safety Guarantees
keyConcepts.content: Code can offer: no guarantee, basic guarantee (invariants preserved), strong guarantee (commit-or-rollback), or no-throw guarantee. RAII is essential for writing exception-safe code.

steps.title: Throwing an Exception
steps.content: The throw statement creates an exception object and initiates stack unwinding. Control transfers to the first matching catch block up the call stack.

steps.title: Unwinding Process
steps.content: For each stack frame: 1) Locate exception table entry for current PC, 2) Run destructors for local objects, 3) Check for catch handler, 4) Pop frame if no handler found.

steps.title: Matching Handlers
steps.content: The runtime checks exception type against catch parameters. Inheritance hierarchies are respected (catch Derived matches Base* handlers). Ellipsis (...) catches everything.

practiceProblems.title: Stack Unwinding
practiceProblems.description: Function A calls B, B calls C, C throws. B has catch, A has catch. Where is the exception caught?
practiceProblems.solution: Caught in B. Unwinding stops at the first matching handler, so B's catch receives control.

practiceProblems.title: RAII & Exceptions
practiceProblems.description: Why does RAII work well with exceptions?
practiceProblems.solution: Destructors are called during stack unwinding, guaranteeing cleanup of resources (memory, locks, files) even when exceptions occur.

minigame.title: Stack Unwinding Challenge
minigame.description: Trace exception propagation through the call stack
